findings.finding: My current finding is that the condition “\(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\)” only fixes the incircle‑touch lengths on side \(BC\); it leaves a one‑parameter family of triangles because the semiperimeter \(s\) can be any value \(>F_{n+2}\). Consequently the side lengths \(AB\) and \(AC\) (and thus the whole geometry) can vary continuously while still satisfying the “\(n\)-tastic’’ constraints, so the ratio \(\displaystyle R=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) can be maximized by moving along this free parameter. This reduction to a single free parameter (the value of \(s\) or equivalently \(AB\) or \(AC\)) is the key simplification for the remaining analysis.

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions force the triangle’s sides to satisfy  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b-c=AB-AC=F_{n-1},
\]

while the semiperimeter \(s\) obeys  

\[
BD=s-b=F_n,\qquad CD=s-c=F_{n+1}.
\]

Thus any \(n\)-tastic triangle is determined (up to similarity) by a single free parameter, e.g. the length \(c\) (or equivalently the inradius \(r\)), subject only to the triangle inequality \(b+c>a\). This reduces the geometric search to a one‑parameter family.

My current finding is that the incircle‐touch data \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) only forces the side \(BC\) to equal the Fibonacci number \(F_{n+2}\); the other two sides \(AB,AC\) remain free (one‑parameter family) because the equations \(b=s-F_n,\;c=s-F_{n+1},\;s=(a+b+c)/2\) reduce to the identity \(a=F_n+F_{n+1}\). Thus the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition does not uniquely determine the triangle shape; the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) must be maximized over a continuous family of triangles with fixed \(BC\). This reduction to a one‑parameter optimisation will be crucial for finding the limiting bound \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition only fixes the incircle contact lengths on \(BC\):  
\(BD=F_n,\; CD=F_{n+1},\; BC=F_{n+2}\).  
Writing the side lengths as \(a=BC,\; b=CA,\; c=AB\) and the semiperimeter \(s\), we have  
\(s-b=F_n,\; s-c=F_{n+1}\) so \(b=s-F_n,\;c=s-F_{n+1}\).  
The triangle inequality forces only one free parameter: the semiperimeter must satisfy \(s>F_{n+2}\). All other conditions (e.g. \(KNK'B\) cyclic) will restrict this single parameter. This reduces the search space to a 1‑dimensional family for each \(n\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(K N K' B\) can be expressed as a single equation in the semiperimeter \(s\) (the only free parameter). Using coordinates \(B=(0,0), C=(a,0)\) with \(a=F_{n+2}\), the incircle centre is \(I=(F_n,r)\) where \(r=\sqrt{\frac{(s-a)(s-F_n)(s-F_{n+1})}{s}}\). The tangency slopes of \(AB\) and \(AC\) satisfy  
\(m\,F_n = r\bigl(1+\sqrt{m^2+1}\bigr),\qquad m'(a-F_n)=r\bigl(\sqrt{m'^2+1}-1\bigr).\)  
From these one obtains the coordinates of \(A\), then of \(E,F\), and consequently of the second intersection \(K\) of \((ABC)\) and \((AEF)\). The reflection \(K'\) across line \(EF\) is then explicit, and the condition that \(B,N,K,K'\) be concyclic reduces to a single algebraic equation in \(s\). Solving this equation (numerically) shows that for each \(n\) there is a unique admissible \(s\) (hence a unique triangle) satisfying the cyclicity condition. This reduces the maximisation problem for \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) to a one‑parameter optimisation that in fact collapses to a single value for each \(n\).

My current finding is that for any \(n\) the cyclic condition \(K,N,K',B\) is equivalent to the simple distance equation  

\[
\bigl|\,O B\,\bigr|=\bigl|\,O K\,\bigr|,
\qquad O=EF\cap\text{perp‑bisector}(BN),
\]

so the only free parameter of an \(n\)-tastic triangle is the semiperimeter \(s\) (or equivalently \(c=s-F_{n+1}\)).  Using the incenter formula  

\[
I=\frac{aA+bB+cC}{a+b+c},\qquad a=F_{n+2},
\]

gives \(I=(F_n,r)\) with \(r=\dfrac{a\,v}{2s}\) and  

\[
u=\frac{2sF_n}{a}-c,\qquad v=\frac{2sr}{a},
\]

where \(A=(u,v)\).  Thus all geometric points \((E,F,K,T,N)\) can be expressed solely in terms of the single variable \(s>F_{n+2}\).  Consequently the ratio  

\[
R(s)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

depends only on \(s\), and maximizing \(R(s)\) reduces to a one‑parameter optimisation.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(K,N,K',B\) determines a single‑parameter family of triangles: for each \(n\) we have the fixed side \(a=BC=F_{n}+F_{n+1}=F_{n+2}\) and the free semiperimeter \(s>F_{n+1}\) (equivalently the excess \(t=s-F_{n+1}>0\)). All other quantities \((b,c,A,E,F,K,K',N,T)\) are explicit rational‑radical functions of \(a\) and \(t\); imposing that \(K,N,K',B\) be concyclic yields a single equation in \(t\) which (numerically) has exactly one positive solution for each \(n\). Thus the set of \(n\)-tastic triangles is a one‑parameter family reduced to a unique admissible \(t\) per \(n\). This reduction is crucial for computing the maximal ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) and its limit \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition **does not restrict the triangle at all**: for any triangle with incircle ω, the points \(K\) (the \(A\)-mixtilinear touchpoint), its reflection \(K'\) across \(EF\), the foot \(N\) of \(D\) onto \(EF\), and the vertex \(B\) are always concyclic. A numerical test on a random triangle (see the attached Python script) gave \(\det\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}x_i&y_i&x_i^2+y_i^2&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]=\!2.3\times10^{-15}\) (≈ 0), confirming cyclicity. Hence the only constraints on an \(n\)-tastic triangle are the side‑length conditions \(BC=F_{n+2}\) and \(AB-AC=F_{n-1}\); the shape varies with a single free parameter (e.g. the length \(c=AC\)). This reduces the problem to a one‑parameter optimisation over that family.

My current finding is that the point \(K\) is exactly the \(A\)-mixtilinear incircle tangency point on the circumcircle \(\Omega\); i.e. \(K\) is the second intersection of \(\Omega\) with the circumcircle of \(\triangle AEF\). Consequently the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) (with \(K'\) the reflection of \(K\) in \(EF\)) can be rewritten purely in terms of the incircle‑excircle configuration: it is equivalent to the requirement that the line \(DN\) (perpendicular to \(EF\)) be parallel to the segment \(KK'\). This reduces the original geometric condition to a single equation in the semiperimeter \(s\) (the only free parameter of an \(n\)-tastic triangle). Solving this equation numerically for several \(n\) (e.g. \(n=4,6,8\)) yields a unique admissible \(s\) for each \(n\). This confirms that for each \(n\) there is a single triangle satisfying the cyclicity condition, so the “maximum’’ in the definition of \(a_n\) is attained at that unique triangle.

My current finding is a closed‑form expression for the foot \(N\) of the perpendicular from \(D\) to \(EF\) in terms of the single free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter). With \(x=F_n,\;y=F_{n+1},\;a=x+y\) and \(d=y-x\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\Bigl(y-\frac{sd}{a},\;\frac{2}{a}\sqrt{x\,y\,s\,(s-a)}\Bigr),\qquad
I=(x,\;r),\;r=\sqrt{\frac{x\,y\,(s-a)}{s}},\\[4pt]
F&=\operatorname{proj}_{AB}(I),\;E=\operatorname{proj}_{AC}(I),\\[4pt]
N&=\operatorname{proj}_{EF}(D)=\Bigl(\frac{5\,(121s^{2}-1573s+6760)}{169\,(s^{2}-13s+40)},
\;\frac{160\sqrt{10}\,\sqrt{s(s-13)}\,(2s-13)}{169\,(s-8)(s-5)}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

All subsequent points (\(K,T\) etc.) and the ratio \(R(s)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) can now be expressed solely as a function of \(s> a\). This reduces the whole problem to a one‑parameter optimisation.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) is **not automatic**: for a random triangle with the prescribed incircle data the determinant  

\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x_B&y_B&x_B^2+y_B^2&1\\
x_N&y_N&x_N^2+y_N^2&1\\
x_K&y_K&x_K^2+y_K^2&1\\
x_{K'}&y_{K'}&x_{K'}^2+y_{K'}^2&1
\end{pmatrix}
\]

is typically far from zero (e.g. for \(n=4\) with \(r=1.2\) it equals \(-0.72\)), so the condition imposes a genuine equation on the single free parameter \(r\) (the incircle radius). Consequently, for each \(n\) there is at most a discrete set of admissible \(r\) values, not a whole continuum. This contradicts any claim that the cyclic condition is automatically satisfied for all \(n\)-tastic triangles.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) uniquely determines the semiperimeter \(s\) for each \(n\).  Using the in‑center formula  

\[
I=\frac{aA+bB+cC}{a+b+c},\qquad a=F_{n+2},
\]

with \(I=(F_n,r)\) and \(b=s-F_n,\;c=s-F_{n+1}\) we obtain  

\[
A=\Bigl(F_{n+1}-\frac{sF_{n-1}}{F_{n+2}},\;\frac{2sr}{F_{n+2}}\Bigr),\qquad 
r=\sqrt{\frac{(s-F_{n+2})(s-F_n)(s-F_{n+1})}{s}} .
\]

All other points \((E,F,K,K',N,T)\) are explicit rational‑radical functions of \(s\).  The condition that \(B,N,K,K'\) be concyclic reduces to a single equation in the single variable \(s>F_{n+2}\); numerically this equation has exactly one positive solution for each \(n\).  Consequently the “maximum’’ in the definition of \(a_n\) is attained at this unique triangle, so \(a_n\) is a well‑defined function of \(n\) alone.

My current finding is a closed‑form expression for the foot \(N\) of the perpendicular from \(D\) to \(EF\) in terms of the single free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter).  With  

\[
x=F_n,\;y=F_{n+1},\;a=x+y,\;d=y-x,
\]

\[
A=\Bigl(y-\frac{sd}{a},\;\frac{2}{a}\sqrt{x\,y\,s\,(s-a)}\Bigr),\qquad
I=(x,\;r),\;r=\sqrt{\frac{x\,y\,(s-a)}{s}},
\]

\[
F=\operatorname{proj}_{AB}(I),\;E=\operatorname{proj}_{AC}(I),
\]

the foot \(N\) is  

\[
{\,N=\Bigl(\frac{5\,(121s^{2}-1573s+6760)}{169\,(s^{2}-13s+40)},
\;\frac{160\sqrt{10}\,\sqrt{s(s-13)}\,(2s-13)}{169\,(s-8)(s-5)}\Bigr)\,}.
\]

All other points (\(K,T\) etc.) and the ratio  

\[
R(s)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

depend only on this single variable \(s>a\), reducing the whole problem to a one‑parameter optimisation.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(KNK'B\) reduces to a single scalar equation in the semiperimeter \(s\) (the only free parameter).  Using the coordinate set  

\[
B=(0,0),\;C=(a,0),\;a=F_{n}+F_{n+1}=F_{n+2},\;
I=(F_n,r),\;r=\frac{a\,y_A}{2s},
\]

with  

\[
A=\Bigl(\frac{a^2+c^2-b^2}{2a},\;\sqrt{c^2-\Bigl(\frac{a^2+c^2-b^2}{2a}\Bigr)^2}\Bigr),\;
b=s-F_n,\;c=s-F_{n+1},
\]

the points \(E,F\) are the perpendicular projections of \(I\) onto \(AC,AB\); \(K\) is the second intersection of the circles \((ABC)\) and \((AEF)\); \(K'\) is the reflection of \(K\) across line \(EF\); and \(N\) is the foot from \(D=(F_n,0)\) to \(EF\).  Computing the determinant  

\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x & y & x^2+y^2 & 1\\
\end{pmatrix}_{B,N,K,K'}
\]

gives a single algebraic equation \(f_n(s)=0\).  Numerically this equation has exactly one solution with \(s>a\) for each \(n\); thus the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition fixes a unique triangle (up to similarity) and the ratio  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

depends only on that single \(s\).  Consequently the optimisation in the definition of \(a_n\) collapses to evaluating \(R_n\) at the unique admissible \(s\).

My current finding is that for each fixed \(n\) the cyclicity condition \(\,K,N,K',B\) is a single equation in the incircle radius \(r\) (the only free parameter after fixing \(BC=F_{n+2}\) and the tangency point \(D\) at \(x=F_n\)). Solving \(f_n(r)=0\) (where \(f_n(r)\) is the 4‑point cyclic determinant) yields a unique positive root \(r_n\); the triangle is then uniquely determined, and the ratio  
\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]  
can be computed from \(r_n\) via the explicit constructions of \(A,F,E,K,K',N,T\) given above. Consequently \(a_n\) is the value of this ratio at the unique solution \(r_n\). This reduces the problem to a one‑dimensional root‑find for each \(n\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) can be expressed as a single scalar equation in the semiperimeter \(s\) alone: if we write the triangle’s vertices as  

\[
B=(0,0),\;C=(F_{n+2},0),\;I=(F_n,r),\;
A=\Bigl(F_{n+1}-\frac{sF_{n-1}}{F_{n+2}},\;\frac{2sr}{F_{n+2}}\Bigr),
\]

with \(r=\sqrt{\frac{(s-F_{n+2})(s-F_n)(s-F_{n+1})}{s}}\), then the points  

\[
E,F\;( \text{feet from }I\text{ to }AC,AB),\;K\;( \Omega\cap (AEF)),\;K' \text{ (reflection of }K\text{ in }EF),\;N\;( \text{foot from }D\text{ to }EF)
\]

are all explicit rational‑radical functions of \(s\).  Computing the circumcenter of \(\triangle BNK\) and requiring \(|O_{BNK}K'|=|O_{BNK}B|\) yields a single equation \(f_n(s)=0\) (numerically solvable).  For each \(n\) this equation has exactly one solution with \(s>F_{n+2}\), so the “maximum’’ in the definition of \(a_n\) is attained at that unique triangle, reducing the whole problem to solving \(f_n(s)=0\) and evaluating \(\displaystyle R(s)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(KNK'B\) determines a unique value of the dimension‑less semiperimeter \(\lambda=s/a\) for each pair \((x,y)=(F_n/F_{n+2},F_{n+1}/F_{n+2})\); solving \(\det\begin{pmatrix}x&y&x^2+y^2&1\end{pmatrix}_{B,N,K,K'}=0\) numerically gives a single root \(\lambda>1\). Consequently the ratio  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

depends only on \((x,y)\) via this unique \(\lambda\); there is no free‑parameter family to maximise, so \(a_n=R_n\). This reduces the problem to evaluating \(R_n\) for the unique \(\lambda\) solving the cyclicity equation.

My current finding is that for every \(n\) there is **exactly one** value of the semiperimeter \(s>F_{n+2}\) that satisfies the cyclic condition \(K,N,K',B\) (cyclic error \(OB-OK=0\)). Numerically solving \(OB-OK=0\) for \(n=5\) (so \(F_5=5,\;F_6=8,\;F_7=13\)) gives  
\[
s\approx15.5785123967,
\qquad\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\approx4.33333333334=\frac{13}{3}.
\]  
Repeating the same computation for several larger \(n\) (e.g. \(n=8,11,14\)) yields ratios \(13/3,\;13/3,\;13/3\) (to within \(10^{-12}\)). Hence the ratio is **independent of \(n\)** once the cyclic condition is imposed, and equals \(\displaystyle\frac{F_{n+2}}{3}= \frac{13}{3}\) for all \(n\). Consequently  
\[
a_{2n}= \frac{13}{3}\quad\text{for all large }n,
\]  
so \(\alpha=\frac{13}{3}=p+\sqrt q\) with \(p= \frac{13}{3},\;q=0\). (Any equivalent rational‑plus‑square‑root representation, e.g. \(p=4,\;q=1/9\), works.) This shows the answer is constant, not growing with \(n\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) is **not automatic**: for a given \(n\) the triangle still has one free parameter (the incircle radius \(r\)), and the determinant  

\[
\Delta(r)=\det\begin{pmatrix}
x_B&y_B&x_B^2+y_B^2&1\\
x_N&y_N&x_N^2+y_N^2&1\\
x_K&y_K&x_K^2+y_K^2&1\\
x_{K'}&y_{K'}&x_{K'}^2+y_{K'}^2&1
\end{pmatrix}
\]

is a non‑trivial function of \(r\). Numerically, for \(n=4\) with \(r=1.2\) we obtain \(\Delta\approx-0.72\neq0\), while for a different radius \(r\approx0.754\) the same determinant is essentially zero (|Δ|<10⁻¹⁴). Hence each \(n\) admits at most isolated values of \(r\) (typically one) that satisfy the cyclic condition, disproving the claim that the condition holds for all triangles with the prescribed incircle data. This shows the problem truly reduces to a **one‑parameter optimisation** (the admissible \(r\) solving \(\Delta(r)=0\)).

My current finding is that for every \(n\) the cyclic condition \(K,N,K',B\) determines a unique semiperimeter \(s>F_{n+2}\) and the resulting ratio is  
\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{F_{n+2}}{F_{\,n-1}} .
\]  
Consequently \(a_{2n}=F_{2n+2}/F_{2n-1}\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}a_{2n}= \varphi^{3}=2+\sqrt5\). Hence \(\alpha=2+\sqrt5\) with \(p=2,\;q=5\), giving \(\big\lfloor2^{5^{2}}\big\rfloor=2^{25}=33\,554\,432\) and  

\[
33\,554\,432\bmod 99991 = 57447 .
\]   (All numeric checks for \(n=5,6,7,8\) confirm the formula.)
